B: Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) image confirming iridocorneal adhesion in Peters anomaly. D: Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) image demonstrating keratolenticular adhesion and central corneal opacity confirming Peters anomaly.

panels.figure_caption: Iridocorneal and keratolenticular adhesions. Peters anomaly (PA) classically describes a congenital corneal opacity resulting from an iridocorneal (A, B) or keratolenticular adhesion (C, D). The opacity may be central (C, D) and may take up a small part or the whole of the cornea, or may be eccentric (A, B). It is unreliable to ascribe this term judging only from the clinical picture without making use of ultrasonography, notably ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM; B, D), which helps visualize the structures of the anterior segment and prove or disprove the presence of adhesions (B, D). The use of UBM in A and B shows contact between the cornea and iris (iridocorneal adhesion) and in C and D contact between the cornea and the anterior lenticular surface (keratolenticular adhesions), resulting in disorganization and loss of clarity in the central cornea, confirming the diagnosis of PA. NB. These opacities are avascular (see Figure 3) and in these cases the lens is of a normal size.
in_text_mentions: aper. The designation PA was only used when there was evidence or description of iridocorneal or keratolenticular adhesion resulting in central or eccentric, localized or total corneal opacification (Figure 1). S-CNA was only designated as such if the phenotype was typical of Cornea Plana 2, CNA2 (OMIM 217300 [35]; Figure 2). This entity is characterized by peripheral corneal scleralization but a view of the eye through the center of the cornea is possible, and there is always accompanying cornea plana. CNA2 can be caused by recessive mutation in KERA encoding the keratan sulfate proteoglycan,

Reviewing the literature on chromosome anomalies and associated CCO highlights how confusion may occur when a clinical phenotype is mislabeled or inaccurately presented (Figure 1 and Figure 3). This confusion may prevent useful genotype-phenotype correlations from being identified and the true nature of this spectrum of diseases and associated genes from being revealed. From the data provided, we attempted to summarize associations regarding primary corneal involvement (Table 2). This information may point to possible candidate genes.

Both patients underwent thorough ophthalmological examination under general anesthesia (EUA) within the first six months of life, enabling detailed evaluation of anterior segment abnormalities and associated ocular findings.

plate_findings.evidence: Caption: "The endothelium membrane was entirely absent from the cornea"; in-text mentions also describe defects of Descemet's membrane and the endothelium.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Patient corneal histology from a Peters anomaly case showing absence of the posterior corneal membrane/endothelium, a characteristic manifestation. B: The disease-focused case report identifies this patient corneal histology and the caption specifically documents abnormal Descemet's membrane with multiple-layer structures. These novel changes are not represented in the allowed findings vocabulary. C: Patient corneal histology in the Peters anomaly article shows the captioned multilayered Descemet membrane with pigmented tissue, a specific described histopathologic finding not available in the controlled vocabulary. D: The panel shows patient corneal histology with focal absence of Descemet's membrane in an area of peripheral synechiae, directly supporting a Peters anomaly manifestation.
panels.attribution_text: Ni et al. A novel histopathologic finding in the Descemet's membrane of a patient with Peters Anomaly: a case-report and literature review.. BMC ophthalmology 2015. doi:10.1186/s12886-015-0131-y. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Histological photographs of the cornea. a Bowman’s membrane was completely absent in the middle area of the cornea. The central internal stroma was hypoplastic and the fibers were extremely disarranged without vessels. The endothelium membrane was entirely absent from the cornea. (Periodic Acid-Schiff stain, original magnification × 10). b An abnormal thickness of Descemet’s membrane was present with the “multiple-layer” structures at the peripheral part of the defect. (Periodic Acid-Schiff stain, original magnification × 40). c The “multiple-layer” structures were found in the Descemet’s membrane and pigmented tissues could be found inside the “layers”. (Periodic Acid-Schiff stain, original magnification × 100). d The pigmented cells situated within the cornea stroma and inserted anteriorly with adhesion to the posterior part of the cornea. Absence in Descemet's membrane in the peripheral synechiae area were shown. (Periodic Acid-Schiff stain, original magnification × 100)
in_text_mentions: he sections were examined by light microscopy. On gross examination, the cornea (7 mm × 8 mm) was densely opacified centrally. Descemet’s membrane has multilayered structures containing pigmented tissue, while pigmented stromal cells extend anteriorly and adhere to the posterior cornea.
